newsitem.title: USA: Biomass crops on CRP land eyed for US fuel supply.
newsitem.headline: Biomass crops on CRP land eyed for US fuel supply.

text.p: Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar applauded the idea Wednesday of using Conservation Reserve land to grow biomass crops for making ethanol.
"I think it's a good idea," Lugar, Indiana Republican, said following a hearing where the idea was discussed.

The Agriculture Department, as part of revamping rules for the Conservation Reserve, has requested public comment on whether biomass crops should be permitted and whether to allow periodic, nonemergency haying and grazing.
At present, farmers cannot harvest crops on the land.

During the Agriculture Committee hearing, an Energy Department official said biomass crops, such as grasses and fast-growing trees, could be vital in lowering production costs for renewable fuels and providing enough raw material for large-scale fuel production.

Keith Collins, chief economist at USDA, said biomass crops would be more environmentally beneficial than row crops but USDA wanted public input if they would be compatible with the reserve's goals of water quality and preventing soil erosion.
Collins said biomass prices were so low that a supplement would be needed to make the market attractive.
Collins posed the possibility of a discounted Conservation Reserve payment to farmers who choose to plant biomass crops.
Biomass plants now pay about $5-$10 a ton for vegetation. Collins said prices would have to reach $35-$40 before biomass would pay better than corn.

The Energy Department official said up to 20 billion gallons of ethanol, or 17 percent of current U.S. gasoline consumption, could be produced yearly if 40 million acres were devoted to biomass crops. Corn-based ethanol now totals about one billion gallons a year.
Created in 1985, the Conservation Reserve pays farmers an annual rent to keep fragile land out of production for 10 years. About 36 million acres were enrolled at latest count.
